title: The Crossing
logline: Where the stream has no bridge, people cross by a rope tied to a tree: a run-up, a grip, a swing, an unsteady landing, and then, every time, a moment of standing firm on the far side.

object.note: Object 10 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: From knowing without stopping to think to a single act of letting go: a stream with no bridge, a rope tied to a tree, and the moment of standing firm on the far side.

thread_out.thread: One crossing becomes many: a ferryman's same short lagoon crossing in stillness and in chop, reaching the same bank by a different way each time.

requirements: A real village where a bridgeless crossing is part of daily life
Consent from the community and anyone filmed crossing
Safety oversight; the crew must never encourage a risky crossing

suggestions.name: A hill-country or wet-zone village with a seasonal stream crossing
suggestions.why: Bridgeless stream crossings by rope, log or pole are still part of daily life in some hill-country villages.
suggestions.verify: A specific village and crossing must be identified and confirmed safe to film.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed.

lesson.in_simple_terms: Letting go and being safe are two different moments: you let go of the rope, land shaking, and only then find your footing. The texts use exactly this picture for the decisive change they describe.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: කඹය අත්හරින මොහොතත්, එතෙර ස්ථිරව පය තබන මොහොතත් දෙකකි; අත්හැරීමෙන් පසු මඳක් සෙලවී, ඉන්පසුවයි ස්ථිරව සිටගන්නේ.
lesson.the_teaching: The texts describe the moment of path and fruition as a short, fixed run of mind-moments that comes only after long preparation. Their simile is a man who runs, grips a rope hanging from a branch, swings across a canal, lets go and stands shaking before he finds his footing: the change-of-lineage moment (gotrabhū) lets go of conditioned things, but firm footing comes only with the path itself. The texts add that what the path cuts off (samuccheda-pahāna) does not arise again, unlike what is only held down.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The camera stays with the physical drama of each crossing: the run-up, the grip, the swing, the unsteady first second on the far bank, then the settled stride. A child, a farmer carrying produce and an older person who hesitates each make the same crossing, in low calm water and in high water after rain. Without explanation the viewer sees that releasing the rope and standing firm are two separate moments.

key_terms.en: path process: the single run of mind-moments in which a path and its fruit arise

lesson.caution: Every crossing in the film is ordinary and repeatable, while the texts describe a change that happens once at each stage; the film does not suggest that anyone filmed has made that crossing.
lesson.builds_on: The farmer's knowing worked without stopping to think; this film turns from long preparation to a single act of letting go, which the texts separate from arriving.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
